bib.title: Towards General Agentic Intelligence via Environment Scaling

legacy_report:
SOURCE: Towards General Agentic Intelligence via Environment Scaling (AgentScaler). Runnan Fang, Shihao Cai, Baixuan Li, Jialong Wu et al., Tongyi Lab, Alibaba. arXiv 2509.13311v1, 16 Sep 2025, preprint (no venue).

COVERAGE: 44,454 of 44,454 chars read (14 pages, all of it): abstract, method, experiments, analysis, related work, conclusion, limitation, references skimmed. The paper has no appendix. Text extraction of Table 2 and Fig 4/5 values is partly garbled (see PROBLEMS). Offsets below are approximate page numbers.

CLAIMS (ranked)
1. A function call can be modelled as a read or write operation on a domain database, so an environment can be built automatically from API sets. This is the core design.
 number: none (more than 1,000 domains, from more than 30,000 APIs)
 setup: APIs collected from ToolBench, API-Gen and an internal repo; domains found by Louvain community detection on a tool graph.
 quote: "any function call can be interpreted as a read–write operation over an underlying environmental database D" and "we obtain M domains (exceeding 1,000)" and "API pools ΘF whose size = N (over 30,000)"
 where: p.2-4

2. Pipeline, in order: tool graph edges come from cosine similarity of parameter embeddings above a threshold τ; an LLM then checks each tool pair within a domain; each tool is materialised as Python code over a generated DB schema; tasks come from directed walks on the tool graph.
 number: none
 setup: the authors say the generated schemas for τ-bench domains matched the official implementations, but this was manual inspection only.
 quote: "when generating database structures and formalizing code within specific domains of τ-bench, we observe through manual inspection that our outputs exhibit a high degree of consistency with the official implementations"
 where: p.3-4

3. Verifiable trajectory filtering uses a three-stage funnel: validity control (well-formed turns plus n-gram repetition removal), environment state alignment (final DB equals gold state), and function-call exact match (for read-only sequences, where state checks cannot discriminate).
 number: none
 quote: "Since a tool sequence consisting entirely of read operations without any write operations would cause state-based filtering to fail, we adopt a stricter exact match approach"
 where: p.5

4. Trajectories whose tool calls returned errors are deliberately kept if they still reach the gold goal, to improve robustness.
 number: none
 quote: "we do not filter out trajectories in which tool calls return errors."
 where: p.5

5. Loss is applied only to tool-call tokens and assistant responses; user turns and tool responses are masked from the loss but stay in context.
 quote: "all tokens in ρi and hi are masked out from supervision but remain visible in the context x<k"
 where: p.5, Eq. 2

6. Two-stage SFT: stage 1 trains general tool use across broad domains; stage 2 specialises in vertical domains. On ACEBench-en, both stages improved over the base model, and stage 2 further raised the Agent subset and the overall score.
 number: none in the text. Fig 3 is a bar chart whose values the extraction does not give.
 setup: base Qwen3-Thinking-30B-A3B, ACEBench-en.
 quote: "through multi-steps agent training in Stage 2, the model's score on the agent set has further improved, and the overall score has also increased."
 where: p.6-7

7. AgentScaler-30B-A3B is competitive with trillion-parameter open models and approaches closed models, but closed models still lead.
 number: τ-bench Retail 70.4, Airline 54.0; τ2 Retail 70.2, Airline 60.0, Telecom 55.3; ACEBench-en Overall 75.7.
 setup: SFT on Qwen3-Thinking-30B-A3B-2507. pass^1 for τ-bench and τ2-Bench; accuracy for ACEBench. Comparators: Kimi-K2-1T 73.9/51.2 (τ-bench), 70.6/56.5/65.8 (τ2), 77.4 (ACE overall); GPT-5-think 78.3/44.0, 81.1/62.6/96.7, 72.2; GPT-o3 70.4/52.0, 80.2/64.8/58.2, 78.2.
 quote: "AgentScaler-30B-A3B 70.4 54.0 70.2 60.0 55.3 76.7 82.7 60.0 75.7"
 where: Table 1, p.7
 note: it does not win everywhere. Kimi-K2 beats it on τ-bench Retail (73.9) and τ2 Telecom (65.8). GPT-5-think scores 96.7 on Telecom against 55.3.

8. The small models gain, but unevenly.
 number: AgentScaler-4B scores 64.3/54.0 (τ-bench), 62.3/56.0/48.2 (τ2) and 65.9 ACE overall, against the Qwen3-Thinking-4B base at 59.1/52.5, 56.1/52.0/28.7 and 49.5. AgentScaler-8B scores 50.4/42.0, 58.8/44.0/45.4 and 67.4, against Qwen3-8B at 45.2/25.0, 41.2/30.5/23.5 and 65.9.
 quote: "AgentScaler-4B 64.3 54.0 62.3 56.0 48.2 70.3 76.7 30.8 65.9"
 where: Table 1
 note: the paper's claim that 4B is "on par with 30B-parameter models" is only partly true. The 4B ACE Agent subset is 30.8, below its own base's neighbours, and 4B ACE Overall equals Qwen3-8B (65.9).

9. Out-of-distribution transfer to ACEBench-zh: all three AgentScaler sizes beat their base on Overall, but not on every subset.
 number: 30B Overall 81.5 (+7.3), 4B Overall 65.6 (+21.7), 8B Overall 73.7 (+2.4). 4B Agent rose from 6.7 to 38.4. 4B Special fell 15.3 and 8B Normal fell 5.1.
 setup: ACEBench-zh, described by the authors as OOD relative to training.
 quote: "AgentScaler-30B-A3B achieves the best overall score of 81.5" and "with its score surging from 6.7 to 38.4 and substantial gain of 21.7 points in the overall score"
 where: Table 2, p.7. The quote says "Qwen3-4B" but the table row is Qwen3-Thinking-4B, so the text is loose.

10. Consistency (pass^k) falls fast as k grows, even for the trained model.
 number: τ2-Bench weighted overall, AgentScaler-30B vs base, k=1..4: 62.5/48.6/38.5/30.6 vs 45.3/34.1/30.9/27.7. Telecom for AgentScaler: 55.3/43.9/30.7/22.8. Airline for AgentScaler: 60.0/46.0/38.0/24.0. Retail for AgentScaler: 70.2/54.4/46.5/41.2.
 setup: τ2-Bench, k independent trials, the task must be solved in all k.
 quote: "a clear downward trend in scores is observed as k increases, suggesting that the stability of existing LLMs remains a considerable challenge."
 where: Fig 4, p.7-8. The pairing of numbers to series is inferred from the extraction order, since Fig 4's numbers are not labelled. Treat with care.

11. Accuracy falls as the number of tool calls per trajectory rises (τ-bench, Retail and Airline), for AgentScaler as well.
 number: none firm. The scatter has noisy small-sample points.
 quote: "there exists a clear negative correlation between the number of tool calls and task accuracy."
 where: Fig 5, p.8

12. Positioning of environment types: real tool environments are costly and unstable; LLM-simulated ones hallucinate and vary; offline state-config environments (τ-bench style) are mostly used for evaluation because they take heavy manual effort. The paper claims automated, rule-validated construction fixes the last point.
 quote: "mocked tool usage in such environments can still interact with real databases or state files through actual execution."
 where: p.8-9

LIMITS
- Authors concede: SFT only, no RL, even though the simulated environment is "inherently well-suited for RL optimization". They validated only up to the 30B scale (nothing above 200B).
- Authors concede long-horizon tool use remains open, and so does low pass^k stability.
- Not shown: no ablation of the filtering funnel or of environment scale (number of domains vs score). The "environment scaling" claim is not tested by varying the scale. No data-volume figure for the training set appears in the text. Stage 1 and 2 effects are shown only on ACEBench-en (Fig 3). No contamination analysis against τ-bench domains (it states its schemas match τ-bench's). User simulator and model not named in the extraction. No variance or seeds reported. 4B and 8B gains are uneven (see claim 8). The paper also says closed models "still maintain a clear performance advantage".
- Dated: the baselines (GPT-5, Kimi-K2, Qwen3-2507) are from mid-2025. The text says "state-of-the-art" for sub-1T open models; check this against newer models before repeating it.

BUILDS ON
tau-bench (Yao et al., 2024) for the interplay and pass^k; tau2-Bench (Barres et al., 2025); APIGen-MT (Prabhakar et al., 2025a) for simulated agent-human interplay; ToolBench/ToolLLM (Qin et al., 2023) and StableToolBench (Guo et al., 2024) for the API pool; API-Gen (Prabhakar et al., 2025b); Louvain (Blondel et al., 2008); SynWorld (Fang et al., 2025) for rewriting API descriptions with explicit input-output specs; StableToolBench-MirrorAPI (Guo et al., 2025) for the read-write framing; ACEBench (Chen et al., 2025); Toolformer (Schick et al., 2023); xLAM (Zhang et al., 2024); ToolACE (Liu et al., 2024a); ToolRL (Qian et al., 2025); Tool-N1 (Zhang et al., 2025); DiaTool-DPO (Jung et al., 2025); Kimi K2 (Team et al., 2025) for tool simulators in data synthesis; Qwen3 (Team, 2025b) as backbone; "era of experience" (Silver & Sutton, 2025); Belcak et al., 2025 on small models.

CODE
Eq. 1, tool graph edge rule (p.3):
E = {(i,j) | sim(ϕ(P_funci), ϕ(P_funcj)) > τ, i≠j}
Eq. 2, masked SFT loss (p.5): L(θ) = −(1/Σ I[k∈T]) Σ I[x_k ∈ T]·log π_θ(x_k | x_<k), where T = tool-call tokens plus assistant-response tokens.
Fig 1 shows a generated tool as `class ProjectSchedulecreate(Tool): def __call__(data, projectDetails) -> str: projects = data["projects"]`.

FIGURES
- Fig 1 (p.3): environment build and agentic task construction. It shows tool doc, domain detection, tool graph, generated DB schema, tool code, user intent, and the initial and gold env state. It explains the whole pipeline at a glance.
- Fig 2 (p.4): simulated user, agent and environment loop, with the interaction trace and final env state each compared to gold. It explains the filtering signal.
- Fig 3 (p.6): bar chart of Stage 1 vs Stage 2 on ACEBench-en (Normal, Agent, Overall).
- Fig 4 (p.8): pass^k, k=1..4, on τ2 domains.
- Fig 5 (p.8): accuracy vs number of tool calls on τ-bench.
Best for the note: Fig 1 and Fig 4. I did not run the captions script, since the text extraction already gives them.

PROBLEMS
- No embedded instructions found.
- Table 2 and the Fig 4 numbers are interleaved in the extraction, so series assignment is inferred. Verify them against the PDF image before quoting the pass^k numbers.
- The text duplicates a reference (Prabhakar 2025a and 2025b are the same paper). The text uses "Qwen3-4B" loosely for Qwen3-Thinking-4B.
- Table 1 headings are not marked as pass^1 inside the table. That is from the setup text only.
- Note for 02-tool-use-and-react.md: the paper is about training data and environments, not prompting-time ReAct. Its bearing is on tool-calling reliability (pass^k decay, long-chain decay) and on verifying a tool call through state-diff checks.
